concepts.title: The First World War and Nationalism in India

questions.q: Using the method 'The First World War and Nationalism in India', work with: price_1914 = 5000, price_1918 = 8000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of price_increase_pct.
questions.a: 60 per cent

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'The First World War and Nationalism in India' and work with: price_1914 = 12000, price_1918 = 5000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of price_increase_pct.
questions.a: -58.3333 per cent

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The First World War and Nationalism in India' refers to.
questions.a: The First World War (1914-1918) created a new economic and political situation in India: increased taxes, forced recruitment, high prices and food shortages caused widespread anger, while the war weakened the myth of British invincibility and strengthened the demand for self-government.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The First World War and Nationalism in India'.
questions.a: The hardships of the First World War -- rising prices, forced recruitment and famines -- turned ordinary Indians against British rule and created the conditions for a mass nationalist movement.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The First World War and Nationalism in India' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The First World War, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement' refers to.
questions.a: The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-1922), launched by Gandhi, aimed to achieve swaraj through peaceful non-cooperation with the British; it was combined with the Khilafat Movement led by the Ali brothers to unite Hindus and Muslims against British rule after the harsh Treaty of Sevres imposed on Turkey.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement'.
questions.a: By joining the Non-Cooperation Movement with the Khilafat cause, Gandhi sought to unite Hindus and Muslims in a single mass movement against British rule, using peaceful methods of boycott and non-cooperation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The First World War, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Civil Disobedience Movement' refers to.
questions.a: The Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-1934), led by Gandhi, was a mass struggle in which people broke colonial laws -- especially the salt law -- by producing salt, refusing taxes and picketing liquor shops; it differed from Non-Cooperation by refusing to obey unjust laws while continuing to remain peaceful.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Civil Disobedience Movement'.
questions.a: Civil disobedience went a step beyond non-cooperation: instead of merely withdrawing cooperation, people openly broke colonial laws they considered unjust, beginning with the salt law at Dandi.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Civil Disobedience Movement' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Towards Civil Disobedience

questions.q: Using the method 'The Salt March (Dandi March)', work with: distance_miles = 240. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of distance_miles.
questions.a: 240 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'The Salt March (Dandi March)' and work with: distance_miles = 240. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of distance_miles.
questions.a: 240 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Salt March (Dandi March)' refers to.
questions.a: The Salt March of 1930 was a 240-mile march led by Gandhi from Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal village of Dandi, where he broke the British salt law by making salt from sea water on 6 April 1930, marking the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Salt March (Dandi March)'.
questions.a: The Salt March turned the simple act of making salt into a powerful symbol of defiance that drew tens of thousands of ordinary Indians into the nationalist struggle.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Salt March (Dandi March)' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Towards Civil Disobedience - The Salt March

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Quit India Movement' refers to.
questions.a: The Quit India Movement was launched by Gandhi in August 1942, demanding an immediate end to British rule; after the arrest of the Congress leaders, the movement became a mass uprising with strikes, demonstrations and attacks on government property, though it was eventually suppressed by the British.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Quit India Movement'.
questions.a: The Quit India Movement of 1942 marked the final mass struggle of the nationalist movement, demonstrating that the Indian people were no longer willing to accept British rule and demanding immediate independence.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Quit India Movement' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Towards Civil Disobedience - Quit India

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Role of Mahatma Gandhi' refers to.
questions.a: Mahatma Gandhi transformed the Indian nationalist movement from an elite constitutional agitation into a mass struggle by introducing the methods of satyagraha (truth-force) and non-violent civil disobedience, uniting diverse groups under the common goal of swaraj.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Role of Mahatma Gandhi'.
questions.a: Gandhi's unique contribution was to make nationalism a mass movement by combining non-violence with active resistance, and by identifying with the everyday concerns of peasants, workers and ordinary people.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Role of Mahatma Gandhi' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Sense of Collective Belonging - Role of Gandhi

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Participation of Different Social Groups' refers to.
questions.a: Different social groups participated in the nationalist movement for different reasons: peasants against high rents and taxes, plantation workers for freedom of movement, business classes against colonial restrictions, and women for the first time in large numbers, each giving the movement its mass character.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Participation of Different Social Groups'.
questions.a: The nationalist movement drew its strength from the participation of diverse groups -- peasants, workers, business classes and women -- each joining for reasons linked to their own social and economic grievances.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Participation of Different Social Groups' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Towards Civil Disobedience - Different Groups

concepts.title: The Sense of Collective Belonging and the Impact of Nationalism

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Sense of Collective Belonging and the Impact of Nationalism' refers to.
questions.a: The sense of collective belonging that united Indians in the nationalist struggle was built through cultural symbols like Bharat Mata, the singing of Vande Mataram, the folklore revival, the reinterpretation of history and the design of the tricolour flag, which together created a shared national identity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Sense of Collective Belonging and the Impact of Nationalism'.
questions.a: Nationalism in India was not only a political struggle but also a cultural process in which symbols, songs, history and images created a shared sense of belonging among diverse people.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Sense of Collective Belonging and the Impact of Nationalism' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Sense of Collective Belonging
